content_list.content_text: In his study of the early sound era titled You Ain't Heard Nothin' Yet, Andrew Sarris describes October 23, 1927, when The Jazz Singer (1927) premiered in New York, as "a date forever marked in film history, as fearfully decisive as Waterloo, Sarajevo or Pearl Harbor." This hyperbolic sentence reflects the systemic nature of the change that sound would bring and the apocalyptic fears of those who believed talkies would diminish the art of film.

information.contentText: Al Jolson's (as Jack Robin) famous line "You ain't heard nothin' yet." was improvised. The film was only meant to synchronize the music, not speech, but Jolson let the line slip after the song "Dirty Hands, Dirty Face " and the director wisely left it in.

content_list.content_text: Sound had been an aspiration since the earliest days of cinema. As early as 1888, Eadweard Muybridge claimed to have discussed with Thomas Alva Edison the possibility of using the latter's sound recording process to accompany his prototype projector, the zoopraxiscope. Throughout the silent era, there were various experiments aimed at bringing mechanically recorded sound to the screen, and two formats gradually evolved: sound-on-disc (in which sound was played on a phonograph in sync with the image) and sound-on-film (in which it was physically recorded on the film on which the image was printed). Although the former method was initially successful, with the Vitaphone process dominating the industry, it was sound-on-film recording that prevailed.

quote.quote: The Jazz Singer brought sound, Lights of New York brought dialogue.
quote.author: Darryl F. Zanuck

content_list.content_text: In 1921, with Dream Street (1921), D. W. Griffith (1875-1948) tried to use the sound process in a feature film. Although it was first released in silent prints, a second version premiered in New York with an introduction narrated by the director himself, as well as a sequence with a recorded song and various sound effects.

information.contentText: Dorothy Mackaill and Milton Sills in The Barker, the inaugural "talkie" (as sound films were called at the time) of First National. The film was released in December 1928, two months after Warner Bros. acquired a controlling interest in the studio.

content_list.content_text: Like Griffith's Broken Blossoms (1919), Dream Street was based on the work of writer Thomas Burke and was set in the same location as the earlier film, London's Chinatown, but it did not achieve the same success. Using an anachronistic sound-on-disc process, Photokinema, Griffith's experiment failed, since most theaters could not accommodate the necessary equipment. The first commercial sound film premiered in August 1926, when Warner Bros. released Don Juan (1926), using the Vitaphone system. Directed by Alan Crosland (1894-1936), the swashbuckler was a mere vehicle for John Barrymore, accompanied by an orchestral score and sound effects recorded on disc.

However, it was The Jazz Singer, also by Crosland, that made the shift to sound irreversible. It may be hard for modern viewers to grasp the impact of this production. Based on the stage play by Samson Raphaelson, this highly mawkish story of a Jewish cantor's son who defies his own father with his desire to sing "jazz" - the film's definition of jazz consists of sentimental ballads and old-fashioned blackface performances - is not exactly a talkie. There is a soundtrack but, with the exception of two sequences, the dialogue is presented through intertitles.

information.contentTitle: Poster for the musical The Broadway Melody (1929)
information.contentText: Premiering on February 1, 1929, MGM's The Broadway Melody (1929) was the first successful talkie from a studio other than Warner Bros., and the first sound film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture.

content_list.content_text: Yet the secret of its success lies precisely in the two talking scenes. In the middle of his act, Jakie Rabinowitz (Al Jolson) introduces the next song with stammering enthusiasm: "Wait a minute, wait a minute, you ain't heard nothin' yet!". Later, as Rabinowitz serenades his mother with "Blue Skies," a 1926 Irving Berlin hit, he breaks off to tell her that if he makes it big, he'll take her to live in the Bronx, "where the Ginsbergs, the Guttenbergs and the Goldbergs live. Oh, a whole lot of Bergs - I don't know 'em all ". Both scenes convey a sense of closeness and intimacy, while Jolson's exhilarating "you ain't heard nothin' yet" offered an irresistible catchphrase for the sound era.
Lights of New York (1928), a Warner Bros. gangster melodrama, was the first all-talking feature film. A hit with audiences, though not with critics, Lights of New York became an unlikely watershed.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Dominic Power, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

content_list.content_text: Technological advances during this period were numerous. The first microphones for recording sound were clumsy and bulky and produced low-quality sound. Technicians insisted that performers stay close to the microphones to get ideal sound quality; this meant that both the camera and the actors stopped moving, resulting in static films that fans and critics alike called "teacup dramas."
content_list.content_title: Production Problems in the Early Years

information.contentTitle: Just Another Day at Work at Warner
information.contentText: This photograph, taken during the making of a Warner Bros film, shows the coordination involved in early sound recording. The scene is simple: a couple talks on a garden bench. They are positioned at the far right of the frame and, in front of them, there are three large wardrobe-like boxes. In the early sound period, cameras had to be placed inside these boxes - or "blimps," as they were called - so that their noise would not be picked up by the microphone. Notice that each box is muffled with large blankets and, in the third one, is the "boom operator," who holds a long pole, the "boom," with a microphone attached to the end, to record the actors' dialogue. He moves this pole left or right depending on which actor is speaking at the moment, and he has to keep it out of the shot at all times. Surprisingly, an orchestra to his left plays while the actors speak. It was only in 1933 that music began to be added separately to a film's soundtrack, after editing. Until then, astonishingly, it had to be recorded simultaneously. A very serious reason not to shoot on real streets.
information.source: George Eastman House / Stills Collection – Motion Picture Department

content_list.content_text: From the filmmakers' point of view, shooting with sound was a whole new game. Real locations were now hard to use, because as soon as the director shouted "Action!", someone nearby would probably start digging up a road or hammering metal. Nobody wanted to hear those sounds while the actors were speaking, so directors and producers were forced to go back to shooting in "black box" studios, which were now called "sound stages."

In the silent era, shooting with more than one camera was used only for big action stunts that could not easily be repeated. For example, if the scene shown in the image above, with the two people sitting in a park, were first shot in a wide shot, followed by close-ups of the man and the woman, it would be very difficult to edit or match the sound of each shot when they were all joined together. The orchestra and the dialogue would have to follow each other with split-second precision - if that didn't happen and the editor cut from a wide shot to a close-up, the sound would come out wrong. The solution was to run three cameras: one shooting the wide shot (in this case, the central camera) and the others shooting the actors' close-ups (in the image, one on the right and the other on the left with the boom operator). The actors, in turn, would have to play the entire scene in one continuous take to ensure that the sound on each camera matched perfectly.

information.contentTitle: Hoping to Stay in the Business
information.contentText: A publicity photo showing young hopefuls approaching the microphone. Many actors were unable to make the transition from silence to sound.

content_list.content_text: Actors' performances were affected by this new technology. The director could no longer speak to them during the take, as had been the norm in silent film, and in the early years of sound, actors had to speak with unnatural precision to be successfully captured by the rudimentary recording technology.

It was only in 1932 in the United States, and later in other countries, that directional microphones were introduced, which could record specific sounds instead of picking up every sound. Note, finally, that the couple on the bench is lit by only two large studio spotlights, one on each side of the trio of cameras. In late silent films, close-ups were lit separately and with great care, in order to create attractive facial shadows and melancholy or romantic backgrounds. In this case, however, that technique is not possible, because the lighting would have to be behind or beside the actors, in place of the bushes. The lights would then be clearly visible in the wide shot, which is filmed at the same time as the close-ups.

information.contentText: Early sound stage with a soundproof booth.

content_list.content_text: Creative directors were immediately frustrated by these obstacles to their artistic freedom, and the best of them devised ways to overcome them. Russian director Rouben Mamoulian (1897-1987) went to the West as a student of the great acting guru Konstantin Stanislavski (1863-1938). First, Mamoulian directed operas in Paris, London and New York, which quickly confirmed that he had no knack for naturalism.

Hired by Paramount on the strength of his inventive stage productions, his first film, Applause (1929), pushed the creative boundaries of sound films. The film's plot was not innovative - a fading stage performer sacrifices her career for her daughter - but a few key scenes made the industry stop and take notice. One example is the contrast between the quiet atmosphere of the convent where the daughter lived and the chaos of the traffic and street noise of bustling New York when she visits her mother; Mamoulian used the sound contrast to reflect the disoriented daughter's feelings.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Martins Fontes, published in the book "História do Cinema" by Martins Fontes

movies.title: The Jazz Singer
movies.overview: A young Jewish man is torn between tradition and individuality when his old-fashioned family objects to his career as a jazz singer. This is the first full length feature film to use synchronized sound, and is the original film musical.

movies.title: M
movies.original_title: M - Eine Stadt sucht einen Mörder
movies.overview: In this classic German thriller, Hans Beckert, a serial killer who preys on children, becomes the focus of a massive Berlin police manhunt. Beckert's heinous crimes are so repellant and disruptive to city life that he is even targeted by others in the seedy underworld network. With both cops and criminals in pursuit, the murderer soon realizes that people are on his trail, sending him into a tense, panicked attempt to escape justice.

movies.title: Love Me Tonight
movies.overview: A Parisian tailor finds himself posing as a baron in order to collect a sizeable bill from an aristocrat, only to fall in love with an aloof young princess.

movies.title: Lights of New York
movies.overview: Eddie is conned into fronting a speakeasy for a local gangster who intends to frame him for the murder of a cop.
